clinicalPearls: Typically affects young to middle-aged adults, more commonly men, presenting with acute or subacute unilateral blurring, a central positive scotoma, micropsia and altered colour perception
Classically associated with type-A personality, psychological stress and exogenous or endogenous corticosteroid exposure, including inhaled, topical and intra-articular routes
Fundus shows a well-circumscribed serous neurosensory detachment at the macula, often with a shallow dome of subretinal fluid and sometimes a small pigment epithelial detachment
Optical coherence tomography demonstrates subretinal fluid separating the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium and is the mainstay for diagnosis and monitoring
Fluorescein angiography classically reveals a focal leak at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium, sometimes with the characteristic smokestack or inkblot pattern of expanding dye
Indocyanine green angiography shows choroidal hyperpermeability and dilated choroidal vessels, supporting the concept of a primary choroidal (pachychoroid) disorder
Most acute episodes resolve spontaneously over weeks to a few months with observation and removal of any steroid exposure
Chronic or recurrent disease can cause widespread retinal pigment epithelial decompensation and permanent visual loss, and may be treated with photodynamic therapy or focal laser to the leakage point
reference.pathophysiology: Central serous chorioretinopathy is thought to arise from choroidal vascular hyperpermeability and congestion (part of the pachychoroid spectrum), which raises hydrostatic pressure beneath the retinal pigment epithelium. This overwhelms and damages the pumping and barrier function of the epithelium, allowing fluid to pass into the subretinal space and produce a localised serous detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula. Corticosteroids and elevated endogenous cortisol are believed to potentiate this choroidal dysfunction, which explains the strong association with steroid use, stress and Cushingoid states. Persistent or repeated fluid accumulation leads to chronic retinal pigment epithelial atrophy and photoreceptor damage.
additionalDifferentials: Wet age-related macular degeneration with choroidal neovascularisation
Optic disc pit with associated maculopathy
Inflammatory or infective posterior uveitis with exudative detachment
Choroidal tumour causing exudative retinal detachment
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography to confirm and quantify subretinal fluid and any pigment epithelial detachment
Fundus autofluorescence to map chronic retinal pigment epithelial changes and gravitational fluid tracks
Fluorescein angiography to localise the focal leak and identify the smokestack or inkblot pattern
Indocyanine green angiography to demonstrate choroidal hyperpermeability and guide photodynamic therapy
Amsler grid testing to document and monitor the central scotoma and metamorphopsia
Review of systemic and topical corticosteroid exposure and screening for hypercortisolism when suspected
redFlags: Failure to resolve over several months or recurrent episodes suggesting chronic disease with progressive atrophy
Features suggesting secondary choroidal neovascularisation such as haemorrhage, lipid exudate or a sudden change in vision
Bilateral or atypical multifocal detachment prompting exclusion of inflammatory, hypertensive or neoplastic causes
Ongoing high-dose corticosteroid exposure that cannot be withdrawn
reference.prognosis: Acute central serous chorioretinopathy usually resolves spontaneously within a few months with good visual recovery, but recurrences are common. Chronic or repeated disease may cause irreversible retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, photoreceptor loss and secondary neovascularisation, with lasting reduction in acuity and quality of vision.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing chronic disease as wet macular degeneration and giving unnecessary treatment, or vice versa
Overlooking occult corticosteroid exposure such as inhalers, skin creams or joint injections
Prescribing corticosteroids for a presumed inflammatory cause and thereby worsening the fluid
Intervening too early in acute cases that would resolve spontaneously, exposing the patient to treatment risk
Failing to recognise secondary choroidal neovascularisation developing on a background of chronic disease
management: Identify and discontinue or taper any exogenous corticosteroid exposure (systemic, inhaled, topical or intra-articular), the key modifiable trigger
Observe acute cases, as most resolve spontaneously, while addressing psychological stress and modifying lifestyle
For persistent or chronic subretinal fluid, reduced-fluence or reduced-dose photodynamic therapy guided by indocyanine green angiography as the definitive treatment
Consider focal laser photocoagulation to an extrafoveal leak localised on fluorescein angiography
Trial a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone or eplerenone in chronic disease
Monitor with serial optical coherence tomography and Amsler grid, and screen for and treat any endogenous hypercortisolism
Refer to a medical retina specialist and watch for secondary choroidal neovascularisation requiring anti-VEGF therapy
